ut_windy_canyon.blurb: A narrow side canyon in Big Cottonwood Canyon, tucked above the Ledgemere picnic area, with fifteen routes on quartzite. Trad leads make up most of the list, with a few bolted lines and a couple of top-rope options. Difficulty runs low to moderate: the bulk of the routes sit between 5.5 and 5.8, and only a couple reach 5.10. Walls stand both low in the gorge and higher up, where the better climbing is said to be, and most of them face east, so expect morning sun. It suits newer leaders and anyone after short, easy days close to the road.
ut_windy_canyon.parking_note: Leave the car in the Ledgemere picnic area lot; the trail into the canyon starts directly across the road from it.
ut_windy_canyon.approach: Cross the road from the lot and follow the trail past a short paved stretch. At the junction, turn north and climb into the canyon; the walk to the first walls takes roughly 10 to 15 minutes.

ut_viewfinder_towers.blurb: A cluster of small, slender sandstone spires beside Utah 24 on the south side of the San Rafael Swell, a short drive from Hanksville. Fifteen routes are listed, nearly all trad, plus one aid line and one bolted route. Most of them fall around 5.9, with a few easier and a handful at 5.10 and 5.11. The rock is a fine-grained, crumbly Entrada sandstone: gentle faces are often badly rotted while the steeper walls tend to hold together better, and the towers west of the road are firmer than those on the east side. Quiet and informal, it is best in the cooler months.
ut_viewfinder_towers.parking_note: A roadside pullout on Utah 24 serves the towers; it has sighting tubes that help you pick out the named spires on the west side of the road.

ut_choss_garden.blurb: A steep sport wall in a gully on the north side of the road in Big Cottonwood Canyon, with about fifteen quartzite routes. The grades are demanding: one route sits in the 5.10s, a handful at 5.11, and most of the rest around 5.12. The wall leans just past vertical and climbs technically, and it is far better than its name suggests, though a few spots carry loose rock. The anchors were replaced with new glue-in hardware in 2022. Expect a talus slog to reach the base, so this crag rewards climbers already comfortable on hard sport routes.

ut_europa_boulder.blurb: A lone, high-quality boulder in the Big Water Boulders of Glen Canyon, in south-central Utah, covered with fun moderate problems. It holds fifteen problems: most are V1 or V2, with one at V0, a V3 that is the standout line, and a few harder ones topping out around V5. Because it stands alone, it makes a self-contained circuit, and the Jupiter Boulder lies a short walk beyond it. A good stop for a mixed group who want plenty of mid-range problems on a single block.
ut_europa_boulder.approach: From the end of the dirt road at the Lo Boulder area, hike east for roughly a quarter mile to reach the boulder.

ut_escape_buttress.blurb: A grayish, south-facing buttress high on the trail in American Fork Canyon, in the southern Wasatch. All fifteen routes here are bolted sport climbs on limestone, in a tight grade range: one at 5.9, eleven at 5.10, and three at 5.11. That makes it a favorite for climbers working through the moderate 5.10s. The wall is sunny, and the bolts are not close together, so it pays to be solid at the grade. The walk in passes other walls in the canyon before rounding a corner to reach it.

vt_deer_leap.blurb: A group of cliffs above Sherburne Pass on US-4 near Killington, set on the ridge the Long Trail follows. Fifteen routes are on record here, nearly all traditional, with two bolted lines. Grades span from 5.4 to 5.12, but the heart of it is the 5.7 range, so it works well for newer trad leaders, with a handful of harder lines above. The main wall is the focus and can feel windy, while a few climbs are suited to top-roping. Expect a scrambly uphill walk to reach the base.
vt_deer_leap.parking_note: Park across the road from the cliff, which sits above the Inn on the Long Trail.
